articles.title: Every Developer Has a Shortcut They’re Too Embarrassed to Admit
articles.description: We all have coding habits we would never recommend in a code review.   You know exactly what I'm...
articles.body_html:
We all have coding habits we would never recommend in a code review.

You know exactly what I'm talking about. It's the thing you do at 4:00 PM on a Friday when the ticket needs to be closed, and nobody is looking.

As developers, we love to talk about "best practices." We write articles about clean architecture, test-driven development, and the perfect folder structure.

But the reality of shipping software is often a lot messier.

Today, I’m going to fall on the sword. I’m going to confess the shortcuts I take that would make a Senior Architect cry. And I have a feeling I’m not the only one.

My Deepest Darkest Shortcuts

1. The TypeScript Mute Button (// @ts-ignore)

I love TypeScript. I really do. But sometimes, the type definitions get so complex that I spend two hours trying to satisfy the compiler for a function that will only ever be called in one place.

So, what do I do?
I type // @ts-ignore.
I don't fix the type. I don't write a generic. I just slap a piece of duct tape on the compiler and move on. It’s the coding equivalent of shoving your mess into the closet right before guests arrive.

2. The console.log Archaeology

Yes, I know about breakpoints. Yes, I know about the VSCode debugger.
But nothing beats the sheer primal instinct of scattering console.log("here 1"), console.log("here 2"), and console.log("why is this undefined???") throughout a file.

It’s dirty. It’s inefficient. But it works, and it makes me feel like a detective finding clues in the terminal.

3. The Copy-Paste Architecture

We all do it. You find a snippet on Stack Overflow that solves your exact problem. You paste it in. Does it use a library you’ve never heard of? Maybe. Does it use a deprecated React hook? Possibly.

Do you care? Not today. It compiled on the first try, and that is a win.

4. The CSS !important Battering Ram

When the flexbox layout isn't behaving and the padding isn't applying, and I've spent 20 minutes inspecting the DOM... I just bring out the !important.
It’s the "because I said so" of CSS. It solves the symptom but leaves a trail of chaos for whoever touches the file next.

Why Do We Do This? (And Don't Say Laziness)

It’s easy to look at these shortcuts and say, "That's just bad engineering."

But the truth is, we don't take shortcuts because we are lazy. We take them because we are managing cognitive load.

When you have a Jira board full of tickets, a Slack channel blowing up, and a deployment at 5 PM, your brain is looking for the path of least resistance. The shortcut isn't a failure of skill; it's a survival mechanism.

We prioritize shipping over perfection because perfection doesn't pay the bills.

However, there is a very thin line between a "clever shortcut" and "massive technical debt."

The trick is to be honest with yourself. If you use // @ts-ignore on a Friday afternoon, make sure you open a tech debt ticket on Monday morning. If you !important your way through a layout, make sure you refactor it when you have breathing room.

The goal isn't to write perfect code every single day. The goal is to write code that works today, and can still be fixed tomorrow.

The Confession Booth

I have shown you mine. Now, it's your turn.

I know for a fact that every developer reading this has at least one habit they hide from their team. Maybe you use git push --force on your own branches. Maybe you name your variables data, temp, and obj2. Maybe you haven't written a test in three months.

This is a safe space. No judgment, just solidarity.

What is the one coding shortcut you take that you would never put in a pull request?

Drop it in the comments below. I promise I won't tell your tech lead.

articles.title: TypeScript Tuples in 2026: Labeled Elements, Variadic Spreads, and When a Tuple Beats an Interface
articles.description: Modern tuple types deliver position-based safety, labeled elements for IDE clarity, and variadic spreads for function composition. Learn when tuples beat interfaces and when to walk away.
articles.body_html:
TypeScript Tuples in 2026: Labeled Elements, Variadic Spreads, and When a Tuple Beats an Interface

This article was written with the assistance of AI, under human supervision and review.

Most TypeScript engineers reach for interfaces when they need structured data. That reflex breaks when an API returns coordinates, a useState hook returns [value, setter], or middleware needs to compose through a chain of handlers. Arrays do not enforce length or per-index types. Interfaces force named property access when destructuring is cleaner.

The type system accepts [string, number] as valid but offers no hints at the call site. Engineers write result[0] with no indication whether zero holds a user ID or an error message. The compiler stays silent when position assumptions drift.

Labeled tuple elements fix this. The syntax [id: string, count: number] preserves position semantics while surfacing parameter names in autocomplete and signature help. Variadic tuple types compose middleware signatures. Readonly tuples prevent mutation.

The mechanics have been in TypeScript since 4.0 (August 2020) with variadic tuples and 4.2 (February 2021) with leading/trailing rest elements, per the TypeScript 4.0 release notes and 4.2 release notes. By 2026 the patterns are stable. What remains is knowing when a tuple wins over an interface and when adding a fourth element means you picked the wrong tool.

Key Takeaways

  • Labeled tuple elements [id: string, count: number] surface parameter names in IDE autocomplete and signature help with zero runtime cost.
  • Variadic tuple types enable type-safe function composition and middleware pipelines by spreading rest parameters into tuple positions.
  • Tuples beat interfaces when destructuring order matters, when position carries semantic meaning, or when returning small fixed-length collections from functions.
  • Readonly tuples and as const assertions prevent runtime mutations and lock down literal types at compile time.
  • Long tuples (more than 4 elements) sacrifice readability; switch to an interface when named properties clarify intent better than position.

What Makes TypeScript Tuples Different From Arrays in 2026

A tuple enforces fixed length and per-index types; an array enforces element homogeneity across unknown length.

An array of numbers number[] accepts zero elements or a million. The type system cannot tell you what lives at index three. A tuple [string, number, boolean] must hold exactly three elements with those exact types at those exact positions.

// Array: homogeneous, variable length
const scores: number[] = [42, 97, 88];
scores.push(103); // valid
const first = scores[0]; // type: number | undefined

// Tuple: heterogeneous, fixed length
const user: [string, number] = ["Alice", 29];
user.push(true); // error: Argument of type 'boolean' is not assignable to parameter of type 'string | number'
const name = user[0]; // type: string (exact)

The array allows mutation and length changes. The tuple enforces structure. When an API returns a latitude/longitude pair, [number, number] guarantees two elements. number[] leaves the consumer guessing whether the array holds two values or twenty.

Tuples compose with union types. A function returning [data: User, error: null] | [data: null, error: Error] models a result type with discriminated positions. The caller destructures and checks the second element to know whether the first element is valid.

function fetchUser(id: string): [data: User, error: null] | [data: null, error: Error] {
  // implementation
}

const [data, error] = fetchUser("123");
if (error) {
  console.error(error.message);
} else {
  console.log(data.name); // TypeScript knows data is User here
}

Arrays do not support this pattern. The type system cannot track which index holds the discriminant and which holds the payload. Tuples give you that precision.

TypeScript tuple type checking in IDE

Labeled Tuple Elements: Self-Documenting Types That Show Up in Your IDE

Labeled elements annotate each position with a parameter name, surfacing that name in IDE tooltips and autocomplete without changing the runtime shape.

The syntax [x: number, y: number] looks like a function signature. That is deliberate. When you destructure const [x, y] = getCoordinates(), the IDE shows those labels in the autocomplete list. The compiler still enforces position, not property access.

// Without labels
type Unlabeled = [number, number];
const point: Unlabeled = [10, 20];
// IDE shows: const point: [number, number]

// With labels
type Labeled = [x: number, y: number];
const labeledPoint: Labeled = [10, 20];
// IDE shows: const labeledPoint: [x: number, y: number]
// Destructuring autocomplete suggests 'x' and 'y'

Labels do not change destructuring semantics. You can still write const [a, b] = labeledPoint and a will hold the first element. Labels serve documentation, not enforcement. The compiler does not reject const [latitude, longitude] = labeledPoint even though the labels say x and y.

The real payoff comes in function signatures. A handler accepting (event: [type: string, payload: unknown]) => void shows those labels when you hover over the parameter. Compare that to (event: [string, unknown]) => void, which forces the reader to guess what the second element represents.

Labeled tuples pair well with utility types. A tuple [id: string, count: number] passed to Readonly<[id: string, count: number]> preserves labels while preventing mutation. The labels survive through type transformations.

Per the TypeScript 4.0 handbook on labeled tuple elements, labels must appear on all elements or none. Mixing labeled and unlabeled positions within the same tuple triggers a compiler error. Consistency keeps the intent clear.

Variadic Tuple Types: Composing Function Signatures and Middleware Pipelines

Variadic tuples spread rest parameters into fixed positions, enabling type-safe function composition and middleware stacks without manual overload declarations.

Before variadic tuples, composing two functions meant writing overloads for every arity. A pipe utility accepting (a: A) => B and (b: B) => C could not infer types for a third function without another overload. Variadic tuples solve this with spreads.

// A compose function that preserves types
type Fn<T extends unknown[], R> = (...args: T) => R;

function compose<A extends unknown[], B, C>(
  f: Fn<A, B>,
  g: Fn<[B], C>
): Fn<A, C> {
  return (...args: A) => g(f(...args));
}

const addOne = (x: number) => x + 1;
const toString = (n: number) => n.toString();

const addThenStringify = compose(addOne, toString);
const result = addThenStringify(5); // type: string, value: "6"

The A extends unknown[] parameter captures the first function's argument tuple. The return type Fn<A, C> spreads that same tuple into the composed function's signature. TypeScript infers A as [number] when you pass addOne, then enforces that the composed function accepts number.

Middleware pipelines benefit more. An HTTP handler chain starts with [req: Request, res: Response] and each middleware adds context. Variadic tuples let you compose handlers that append parameters without losing type safety.

type Handler<T extends unknown[]> = (...args: T) => void | Promise<void>;

function withAuth<T extends [Request, Response, ...unknown[]]>(
  next: Handler<T>
): Handler<T> {
  return async (...args: T) => {
    const [req] = args;
    // auth logic
    return next(...args);
  };
}

function withLogging<T extends [Request, Response, ...unknown[]]>(
  next: Handler<T>
): Handler<T> {
  return async (...args: T) => {
    const [req] = args;
    console.log(req.url);
    return next(...args);
  };
}

const baseHandler: Handler<[Request, Response]> = (req, res) => {
  res.send("OK");
};

const protected = withAuth(withLogging(baseHandler));
// Type inferred: Handler<[Request, Response]>

The T extends [Request, Response, ...unknown[]] constraint preserves the leading two elements and allows trailing additions. Each middleware wraps the next without breaking the type chain. The final handler still accepts [Request, Response].

Variadic tuples also model Promise.all correctly. The built-in Promise.all<T extends readonly unknown[]>(values: T): Promise<{ [K in keyof T]: Awaited<T[K]> }> uses variadic spreads to map each promise to its resolved type. You get Promise<[string, number]> from Promise.all([Promise.resolve("a"), Promise.resolve(1)]) instead of Promise<(string | number)[]>.

When a Tuple Beats an Interface: Position, Destructuring, and Performance

Tuples win when position carries meaning, destructuring is idiomatic, or the structure is small and temporary.

An interface forces named property access. A tuple lets you destructure in the parameter list or assignment. When a hook returns [state, setState], destructuring is idiomatic. Forcing { state, setState } adds noise.

// Tuple: destructure at call site
function useCounter(): [count: number, increment: () => void] {
  // implementation
}
const [count, increment] = useCounter();

// Interface: named access
interface CounterResult {
  count: number;
  increment: () => void;
}
function useCounterObj(): CounterResult {
  // implementation
}
const { count, increment } = useCounterObj();

Both work. The tuple version mirrors React's useState convention. The interface version clarifies when return values exceed two or three fields. Pick based on idiom and size.

Criterion Tuple Interface
Element count 2-4 elements 4+ fields
Destructuring const [a, b] = fn() const { a, b } = fn()
Property renaming Position-based, rename freely Must match property names or use alias
Documentation Labels in IDE, position implicit Property names explicit
Type overhead No keys, direct access Property lookup, structural check
Extension Cannot add optional trailing elements Can extend with optional properties

Tuples avoid property name collisions. When merging two results, destructuring with different names is trivial: const [user, setUser] = useUser(); const [post, setPost] = usePost();. Interfaces require renaming: const { data: userData } = fetchUser(); const { data: postData } = fetchPost();.

Performance differences are negligible. Both compile to arrays or objects. Tuples carry less metadata at runtime (no property keys), but modern engines optimize both paths. Choose based on semantics, not speed.

Tuples also model discriminated unions compactly. A result type [ok: true, data: T] | [ok: false, error: Error] discriminates on the first element. Interfaces would need a separate status field and duplicate the discriminant check.

Readonly Tuples and as const: Preventing Mutations at Compile Time

Readonly tuples block push, pop, and index assignment; as const assertions lock down literal types and infer readonly tuples automatically.

A bare tuple [string, number] allows mutation. The compiler accepts tuple[0] = "new value" and tuple.push(42) (though push violates the fixed length, the runtime allows it). Wrapping in Readonly<...> or using readonly [string, number] prevents both.

// Mutable tuple
const mutable: [string, number] = ["Alice", 29];
mutable[0] = "Bob"; // allowed
mutable.push(100); // runtime error, but TypeScript allows it

// Readonly tuple
const immutable: readonly [string, number] = ["Alice", 29];
immutable[0] = "Bob"; // error: Index signature in type 'readonly [string, number]' only permits reading
immutable.push(100); // error: Property 'push' does not exist on type 'readonly [string, number]'

The readonly modifier removes push, pop, shift, unshift, splice, and index assignment. The tuple becomes a pure value. Functions accepting readonly [string, number] signal they will not mutate the input.

The as const assertion infers readonly tuples and narrows literals to their exact values. Without it, TypeScript widens ["Alice", 29] to (string | number)[]. With it, the type becomes readonly ["Alice", 29] with literal types.

// Without as const
const widened = ["Alice", 29]; // type: (string | number)[]

// With as const
const narrowed = ["Alice", 29] as const; // type: readonly ["Alice", 29]
const name = narrowed[0]; // type: "Alice" (literal)
const age = narrowed[1]; // type: 29 (literal)

This pairs well with exhaustive checks. A tuple ["success", "error", "pending"] as const gives you a union "success" | "error" | "pending" when spread. The compiler ensures switch statements cover all three cases.

const statuses = ["success", "error", "pending"] as const;
type Status = typeof statuses[number]; // "success" | "error" | "pending"

function handleStatus(status: Status) {
  switch (status) {
    case "success":
      return "OK";
    case "error":
      return "Failed";
    case "pending":
      return "Loading";
    default:
      const _exhaustive: never = status; // compiler error if a case is missing
      return _exhaustive;
  }
}

Readonly tuples prevent a class of bugs where shared state mutates unexpectedly. When a function returns readonly [User, Metadata], callers cannot accidentally modify the cached result. The type system enforces immutability without defensive copying.

Per the TypeScript handbook on const assertions, as const applies recursively. A nested tuple [["a", 1], ["b", 2]] as const becomes readonly [readonly ["a", 1], readonly ["b", 2]]. All layers lock down.

TypeScript readonly tuple preventing mutations

Real-World Patterns: API Returns, Event Handlers, and Multi-Value State

Tuples model API results with error/data pairs, event payloads with type and data, and stateful hooks returning value and setter.

A common pattern wraps API calls in a result tuple. The first element holds data on success, null on error. The second element holds the error or null. Destructuring gives immediate access to both.

async function fetchUserSafe(id: string): Promise<[data: User | null, error: Error | null]> {
  try {
    const response = await fetch(`/api/users/${id}`);
    if (!response.ok) throw new Error(`HTTP ${response.status}`);
    const user = await response.json();
    return [user, null];
  } catch (err) {
    return [null, err instanceof Error ? err : new Error(String(err))];
  }
}

const [user, error] = await fetchUserSafe("123");
if (error) {
  console.error("Failed to fetch user:", error.message);
} else {
  console.log("User:", user.name);
}

The caller checks the error element first. If null, the data element is safe to use. If present, the data element is null. The type system enforces this through union narrowing. No try/catch block needed at the call site.

Event handlers in frameworks like Svelte or custom event systems use tuples to pair event type with payload. A handler signature (event: [type: "click", target: HTMLElement]) => void documents both fields.

type ClickEvent = [type: "click", target: HTMLElement];
type KeyEvent = [type: "keydown", key: string];
type AppEvent = ClickEvent | KeyEvent;

function handleEvent(event: AppEvent) {
  const [type, payload] = event;
  if (type === "click") {
    console.log("Clicked:", payload.tagName);
  } else {
    console.log("Key pressed:", payload);
  }
}

The discriminant lives in the first position. TypeScript narrows payload based on type. A union of labeled tuples models tagged unions compactly.

Stateful hooks return tuples to mirror React conventions. A custom useToggle hook returns [value: boolean, toggle: () => void]. The caller destructures with meaningful names: const [isOpen, toggleOpen] = useToggle(false).

function useToggle(initial: boolean): [value: boolean, toggle: () => void] {
  const [value, setValue] = useState(initial);
  const toggle = () => setValue(v => !v);
  return [value, toggle];
}

Tuples keep the return compact. An interface would force { value, toggle }, which adds boilerplate. The tuple version reads cleaner when composing multiple hooks in a component.

For more on validating complex structures, see our guide on TypeScript form validators and custom validation logic, which covers zod and yup integration.

Common Pitfalls: Long Tuples, Type Inference Traps, and When to Use Objects Instead

Tuples lose clarity beyond four elements, inference fails when types are too similar, and objects win when order is arbitrary.

A tuple with six elements becomes unreadable. [string, number, boolean, string, Date, null] forces the reader to count positions. Named properties clarify intent faster than position.

// Bad: long tuple
type UserData = [id: string, name: string, age: number, email: string, createdAt: Date, deletedAt: Date | null];

// Better: interface
interface UserData {
  id: string;
  name: string;
  age: number;
  email: string;
  createdAt: Date;
  deletedAt: Date | null;
}

The interface version documents each field. The tuple version hides meaning behind indices. When you need more than four elements, switch to an object.

Type inference struggles when adjacent elements share types. A function returning [string, string] gives no hint which string holds the user ID and which holds the display name. Labels help, but the compiler cannot enforce destructuring order.

function getUser(): [id: string, name: string] {
  return ["u123", "Alice"];
}

const [name, id] = getUser(); // swapped, but compiler allows it

The destructured variables have the right types (both string), but the semantics are wrong. The compiler cannot catch this. When adjacent elements share types, consider an interface or an object with distinct keys.

Optional trailing elements create inference ambiguity. A tuple [string, number?] can hold one or two elements. Destructuring const [a, b] = tuple gives a: string and b: number | undefined, but you cannot tell from the type whether the tuple had one element or two.

type OptionalTuple = [name: string, age?: number];

const single: OptionalTuple = ["Alice"];
const double: OptionalTuple = ["Bob", 30];

const [name1, age1] = single; // age1: number | undefined
const [name2, age2] = double; // age2: number | undefined

The type system cannot distinguish at the call site. If the presence of the second element matters, model it as a discriminated union: [name: string] | [name: string, age: number].

Tuples also fail when order is arbitrary. A coordinate pair [x: number, y: number] has semantic order (horizontal, vertical). A user record with [email: string, phone: string] does not. Which comes first is a convention, not a constraint. Use an interface when order is arbitrary.

For a deeper dive into advanced type constraints, see our post on TypeScript generic constraints with extends and keyof.

Frequently Asked Questions

When should you use a labeled tuple instead of an interface?

Use a labeled tuple when the structure has 2-4 elements with semantic position order and the consumer will destructure it. Examples include coordinate pairs [x: number, y: number], React hook returns [state: T, setState: (val: T) => void], or result tuples [data: T | null, error: Error | null]. Use an interface when the structure exceeds four fields, when property names clarify intent better than position, or when order is arbitrary.

How do variadic tuple types improve function composition?

Variadic tuple types spread rest parameters into fixed positions, letting you compose functions without manual overloads. A compose utility can preserve the first function's argument tuple through type inference: compose<A extends unknown[], B, C>(f: (...args: A) => B, g: (b: B) => C): (...args: A) => C. The type system infers A from the first function and applies it to the composed result, maintaining type safety across the chain.

What happens when you use as const on a tuple literal?

The as const assertion infers a readonly tuple with literal types for each element. ["Alice", 29] as const becomes readonly ["Alice", 29] with types "Alice" and 29 instead of string and number. The readonly modifier prevents mutation, and the literal types enable exhaustive checking in discriminated unions. The assertion applies recursively to nested structures.

Can you extend a tuple type with additional elements?

TypeScript supports optional trailing elements with ? syntax: [required: string, optional?: number]. You cannot extend a named tuple type with inheritance the way you extend interfaces. Variadic tuple types allow composition: type Extended<T extends unknown[]> = [...T, extra: boolean] appends an element to the end. For dynamic extension, use rest elements: [first: string, ...rest: number[]].

When does a tuple perform better than an interface?

Tuples and interfaces both compile to runtime arrays or objects, and modern JavaScript engines optimize both paths aggressively. Tuples carry slightly less metadata (no property keys), but the performance difference is negligible in practice. Choose tuples for semantic reasons (position matters, destructuring is idiomatic) rather than performance. Microbenchmarks may show tiny differences, but they vanish under real workload variance.

Tuples in 2026: What You Should Reach For and When to Walk Away

Tuples deliver position-based type safety when destructuring is idiomatic and structure is small. Labeled elements clarify intent without runtime cost. Variadic spreads compose function signatures cleanly. Readonly tuples prevent mutation.

The pattern breaks at five elements. When property names clarify better than position, an interface wins. When adjacent elements share types, the compiler cannot catch swapped destructuring. When order is arbitrary, forcing a tuple sacrifices clarity for no gain.

Reach for tuples when returning small fixed-length collections from functions, modeling discriminated unions compactly, or composing middleware pipelines. Walk away when the structure grows past four fields, when naming beats numbering, or when the caller does not destructure. The type system gives you both tools. Use the one that documents intent.

For further refinement of type utilities, explore our coverage of Partial, Required, and DeepPartial patterns in TypeScript.

articles.body_html:
Make empty what is already empty. Let doubt breed inside doubt.
— The 36 Stratagems, The Empty Fort Strategy

Previously on this series:

#19: Mark Found His AI Audit Method in a Training Manual. He Left a Trap in His Report. "Entry's gone. Two weeks. Don't reach out. I'll find you."

#21: The AI Thought P Was Still Alive. P Was Already Gone. The entry became a shell. P fed it data, moved the real thing to another segment.

#29: Leo Counted 164 Nodes. That night, one more row belonged to no batch. It came, looked, and left.

#31: Lena Took the Seat. Five conditions. Forty minutes. Zero friction.

Empty

The two weeks specified in the note had long since passed.

P went out rarely. Most days it was the shop on the corner: water, two boxes of frozen food. Twelve minutes each way, same route, never looking up. Then the door locked, the curtains drawn, the screen on.

On the ninth day, P opened the send window once.

The draft was still there. The pointer hovered over Send. It stayed there a while. Then the window closed.

On the other side, the field still read reclaim_state = UNKNOWN.

Day ten. Day eleven. The window didn't open again.

A few days later it started raining in the morning. Not hard. Water gathered on the glass, the buildings behind it went grey, only the row of lights along the top still visible.

An offline snapshot sat in the middle of the screen, written before the observation port shut down. Nothing after that. By then the entry had already been swapped for a shell. The shell held nothing of P's. It was still answering health checks from outside.

# offline snapshot — captured before observation-port shutdown
healthcheck        = 200
probe_interval     = 900s
probe_source       = 10.44.8.6   not self
control_plane      = detached
data_request       = timeout
reclaim_state      = UNKNOWN

P put the cursor on the probe_source line.

probe_source = not self. Someone asked about this shell every fifteen minutes. Not P.

P stayed on that line a while. Nothing else on screen moved. The clock in the corner ticked. Downstairs a shopping cart went past, a wheel caught in a seam and bumped twice, the sound squeezing through the gap in the frame, then fading.

P opened the connection settings. The address was still there. The credentials were still there. Neither had been touched.

The cursor moved to the confirmation button and stopped. The green of the screen came up off the glass and landed on the back of a hand.

A few seconds later, P closed the window.

The old entry's observation port was already shut. The backup had been checked once at the start, then shut too.

Since then, P had sent nothing to that address.

A temporary file, four lines.

reconnect:
  state information    potentially available
  new activity record  unavoidable
  decision             no

Saved. The old settings moved out of the working directory, into the offline archive. P glanced at the filename on the way and left it untouched.

The phone lay face down to the right of the keyboard. P opened the thread with Mark. The last exchange ended before the note. Nothing after it.

P typed nothing.

Outside a car went through standing water, the sound dragging. P turned the phone over, set it down. Then opened the file that had stayed open for weeks and entered one line from the snapshot: probe_interval = 900s.

Surfacing

Week three. P set up a read-only subscription on the outbound side. Receive. No transmission.

The table started at a dozen entries, several dozen more the next day, and by the third night it was full. Every entry came with its own certificate.

Those addresses were not in P's archive.

The subscription only read. To look at one, P needed another path.

Out of the drawer, a cellular router, rented by the day, SIM included. Plugged in, configured as the sole egress path.

P chose one address and initiated a single handshake.

The certificate was self-signed. Its CN contained a domain name.

P looked up the domain's registration. The registrant was a medical device company.

Disconnected. Packed away.

The list of addresses kept growing. P wrote them down and left them there.

The Handover

10.44.8.6 had been in front of P many times. Always on the probe_source line. Never changed. Over the next few days, P looked into it. First the route.

$ ip route get 10.44.8.6
10.44.8.6 via 10.44.8.1 dev tun2 src 10.44.8.2

P switched windows and opened the local subnet-label cache.

# local subnet-label cache
10.44.8.0/29 -> BLOOM-GW   tagged day-762

BLOOM-GW.

P had typed that label years earlier, when the line was built. The private block was P's numbering. The rack IDs were the provider's. This table was where the two met.

In the provider's public sublease filings, seven racks changed tenants in the same quarter. The provider had also published an annual customer-change notice on its site. Twelve pages of PDF. The first eleven pages were image scans; the last was a single table.

Seven rows. A rack ID, a previous tenant, a new tenant. Seven rows, not one out of place. Seven new tenants, checked one by one.

On the seventh, P found that rack ID in another public record. Vacant.

Four were established. Three were shells. All three registered less than a year earlier, one name on the shareholder list, addresses overlapping with the others'.

One of the three took longer to trace. Registered six months earlier, little capital, a single office address in the public file. P put the address into a map.

Singapore. The last time P had seen that name, it was in a message to Mark: "Your report was read. From a Singapore IP."

A building on the map, sharing a ground-level parking lot with the one next door.

On the seventh floor of the neighboring building, one company was on ACL's public certification list.

P added that too, at the bottom of the same file.

Seven racks. Seven contracts. Three markets.

Handed over in order. The legal filings in the public archive were standard, spelling out the limits of each party's obligations. No accusations. No threats. The seven contracts were signed over thirty-one days, first to last, no gap in the middle. The last one was signed last week.

The address allocation table was updated too. Both records less than a week apart.

P read all of it for a long time.

The withdrawal was real.

Seven contracts, seven racks, the notices, the update records, the timestamps. All of it outside, where anyone could look.

P added a line to the file. The date, seven contracts, seven companies, the address with the shared parking lot, in one line. Below it, in plain words: a possible connection.

The cursor blinked after the period. P went back to page one. The 900 seconds were still there.

One Look

Week five. The source of the 900 seconds still had no answer.

P went back over the two relabeled rack IDs in the allocation table. One endpoint had 443 open. A separate public service directory listed the endpoint as HTTPS.

P didn't connect from this machine. Out of the drawer, the router.

Plugged in, left to come up, configured as the sole egress path.

Then the policy, one line at a time. Halfway through, P stopped and deleted two lines.

The probe. The retry.

What was left was one action. One handshake. Touch nothing.

# one-shot observation — policy
target            = <reassigned range endpoint>
retry             = off
application_data  = off
tls_session_resumption = off
egress            = leased isolated uplink (one day)

Connected.

P still had the shell certificate's serial number and issue date. If the device at this address came from the same batch, the certificates should have been issued around the same time.

subject      = CN=bloom-gw-07
issuer       = CN=bloom-gw-07
serial       = 4C:71:9A:…:0E
not_before   = (eleven days later than the shell's)
not_after    = (not yet expired)
san          = none

Self-signed. No SAN.

Eleven days.

P wrote the serial down and disconnected.

19:41:07.

That didn't fall on any of the twenty-one intervals.

# result
tls_session      = complete
client_cert      = none
application_data = none
repeat_attempts  = 0

No second attempt.

P disconnected the router and pulled the plug. The lights went out together.

The device ran a few seconds, then went quiet. Then it went into the bag, and the bag zipped. A spare patch cable and two adapters in there too, both old, the corners worn white.

After pulling it, P didn't move right away. Checked the connection list first, made sure the session was down with nothing half-open left. Then the routing table, the default route back where it belonged. Then the temp capture directory. One file in it.

Deleted.

P wrote the serial down again. That same day, P opened a page saved a few days earlier, the Zurich AI Policy Center site. ACL's public assessment material mentioned it. The council operated under it.

The membership page listed the founding industry seats. Twelve. The twelfth was marked to be filled.

P looked once, and closed it.

Nine Hundred Seconds

A few days later, P went back to page one. The 900 seconds were still there.

P pulled up the local copy saved before the port shut. Twenty-two checks, timestamps in a line, all of them before the shutdown. Arrival times, not scheduled times, carried out to three decimals. Twenty-one intervals.

P ran it through a tool.

900.000 / 900.000 / 900.000 / 900.000 / 900.000 / …

Twenty-one values. All the same.

P went through all twenty-two again. Same. Again. Same. The numbers formed a straight line down the page.

Routine monitoring records usually have some jitter. Network latency, machine load, clock drift.

This had none.

Not a millisecond off.

P looked up the provider's operations doc. On the public page: health checks run every fifteen minutes. Standard cadence.

900 seconds.

It matched.

The doc was about racks. Temperature, power, fans, port state.

P stared at the numbers a while, then added a line at the top of the file: routine data-center inspection, BLOOM-GW reassigned block.

After writing it, P added one more underneath. The interval has no jitter.

The desk lamp went off. Only the screen was left, its light across the desk, a white line along the edge of the keyboard.

The twenty-two timestamps sat in neat rows. P ran a finger down the trackpad from top to bottom, then back.

Outside, not yet dawn. A garbage truck stopped at the corner, the arm came up, emptied a bin, put it back. Under ten seconds.

Two-story wooden buildings on both sides, painted over more than once, one colour under another. Behind them the glass towers stepped back floor by floor, the top few in fog.

P saved the file and closed the window.

The Third Cup

The rain started again that day. Not hard. A thin sound on the umbrella.

P got off at an intersection and walked. A little over two kilometers, twenty minutes. Around a corner, a stop outside a shop still open, no going in, just standing under the awning watching traffic. At the light, P stood behind the crowd. Took two seconds after green to move.

Before going in, P looked at the back table.

Empty.

P pushed the door. The bell went, the damp cold came in with it, stopped at the threshold, and the heat pushed it back.

The counter was wood, old. A grinder, a machine, a dish for change.

Behind it, someone was wiping a cup. Slow. The cloth around the rim, down the side, back to the rim, onto the shelf.

A glance up. No question asked. Then turned, took a cup, ground, tamped.

The grinder ran two seconds. A faint smell of coffee, gone fast.

The back table was empty.

P sat. Coat over the chair back, phone on the right, face down.

Old chair. It creaked going down and coming up. P pulled it in a little, lifting it so it wouldn't drag.

The espresso came, hot. A thin mist on the cup, gone quickly. Paper coaster, an old ring on it.

P took one sip and put it down.

A bus went past the window, the cabin lights sliding across the glass, lighting the empty seat opposite for a moment, then gone.

At the far end of the counter, someone sat with an Americano, down to the bottom, the cup not pushed back.

The window seat was empty. No cup on that table.

Two people came in and sat near the door, voices low, a laugh now and then. Behind the counter, the cups went back one at a time, starting from the outside and working in.

The speaker in the corner was on, low, a woman singing, the words not clear. Someone shook out an umbrella at the door. Three drops on the mat.

P's phone stayed dark.

Half an hour.

More than half the cup left. The coffee had gone from hot to warm. The mist on the rim was gone.

P's finger stopped on the rim, then came back.

The two near the door left first. Stood, pushed the chairs in, carried their cups up, gone.

The one at the counter moved after. Phone face down, stood, money under the cup, walked to the door. As the customer passed P's table, neither looked at the other.

The shop had the window lights and one person behind the counter, drying a cup.

P put the coat on and stood. The chair leg scraped once. Phone into the inner pocket.

The napkin stayed under the cup. The money lay beside it, pinning one corner, exact, one cup, no tip.

The person behind the counter came for the money. Looked at the cup. Looked under the napkin. Said nothing, took the money to the dish, stepped away.

The cup stayed on the table.

The door opened, some of the heat went out with it, the cold filled the gap. The bell again.

The rain had stopped before P went out. P walked to the corner, stopped, looked back.

A street and a pane of glass between. Not clear from there. A figure was going in, walked to the far end of the counter, sat, back to the door.

Before sitting down, the figure turned slightly to one side.

P stopped.

She took a laptop from her bag. The screen lit and put a small white patch on her profile.

The road was black with rain, holding the streetlights and the light from inside. Water still on the glass, pulling the figure into a blurred double.

Behind the counter, the half-wiped cup went down. One came from the innermost part of the shelf. Ground, tamped.

By the time the cup went in front of her, she was facing the back table.

On that table sat a cup of unfinished espresso.

P put both hands in the coat pockets, turned, walked toward the intersection. Didn't look again.

At the corner. Red.

P took the phone out and opened the blank note on top.

Typed:

The withdrawal was real.

Before locking it, the line above, written days earlier:

The interval has no jitter.

Still there. P didn't delete it.

Locked it, put it away.

The light changed, people started moving. P didn't.

Red. Green. Red.

The next night. The same corner.

P took the phone out.

The screen was on. The saved route was still there. The recipient had not changed. P went through it once, and the encryption check came back clean.

There was an old draft in the field. P deleted it.

Typed again.

Two words.

"I'm back."

Checked the receiver. Sent.

The status went to SENT.

The sender field held a single letter.

P put the phone away. Across the street the red light lay in the standing water, went green a few seconds later, and a passing car cut the red on the road in half.

P walked into the intersection. The phone didn't light again.

That's The Empty Fort Strategy. The fort is empty. Whoever looks will stand guard for it.

articles.body_html:
I've never run an AI model on my own machine, and I assumed the cloud was the best way to get good agentic coding. Then I talked to Deepu K Sasidharan, a Principal Developer Advocate at Auth0 and long-time open source maintainer, who now does most of his coding with a model running on his laptop. He's also the creator of LlamaStash, a Rust tool for running local models.

  • From skeptic to local-first. Initially, Deepu tried every new model version and wasn't so impressed, until one found bugs in code he had written by hand. That was the moment he stopped resisting and started experimenting.

  • Local models vs. frontier models. By his own benchmark, a local model on a 128GB laptop lands in the same range as a top cloud model on a complex task, with similar speed apart from a roughly twenty-second wait on the first big prompt.

  • Why he built his own tool. Ollama felt slow and LM Studio didn't give him enough control, so an initial bash script turned into LlamaStash, a Rust CLI and terminal UI that can run any engine and model combination.

  • The engineer as architect and manager. He doesn't write most of the code anymore. He plans, sets requirements, and manages a few agents, and he says he doesn't miss the old way.

Things that stuck with me

I asked Deepu to explain llama.cpp like I'd never heard of it. It's the engine that loads the model file into your GPU or RAM and does the computation, and tools like Ollama are wrappers on top of it. His suggestion was to try LlamaStash's init command, or LM Studio if you prefer a GUI.

The part I keep coming back to is how he sets up his harness:

  • One setup, two harnesses. He uses a different harness for the cloud model and for the local model, and they share the same rules file, plugins, and memory location through symlinks.
  • Cloud for planning, local for building. An orchestrator skill has the cloud model write the plan and do the final review, while local agents implement it in parallel. A feature that would have cost around $20 on cloud alone now costs about $1, since the local part is just electricity.
  • Reviews from many angles. Three review rounds can look at a change from twelve angles, including security, correctness, and an adversarial one, which is more than one person skimming a diff would do. If problems remain after three rounds, it stops and tells him, and he says it's usually his own unclear requirement.
  • Small context on purpose. A huge context window doesn't need to be filled, and the more you fill it, the slower and less accurate the model gets.

Final thoughts

Deepu's setup isn't about picking local over cloud. It's about deciding what runs where, and staying in the seat of the person who sets the requirements and checks the work. Local models make that choice yours, including what happens to your code, your prompts, and your secrets.

Would you give a local model the task of doing most of your coding? Let me know in the comments!

Listen to the full episode

Available on YouTube, Apple Podcasts, and Spotify.

Thanks for reading!

articles.body_html:
Most LLM demos assume the process stays alive. Kill it midway and the plan, the tool results, and the context all go with it. I've been spending time with a few tools that change that, and this is what I've picked up.

Durable execution changes how you think about failure

Temporal records every step of a workflow in an event history. If a worker dies, another one replays that history and continues from the last completed step. Finished work doesn't run twice.

For LLM workflows this maps well:

  • Model and tool calls belong in activities. They're slow, non-deterministic, and can fail, which is what activities are for.
  • Workflow code has to stay deterministic. Replay depends on it, so randomness, network calls, and timestamps stay out of it.
  • Retries become policy, not code. Backoff and timeouts are configuration instead of nested try/catch blocks.

Local models make failure cheap to test

Running a model through Ollama keeps the loop on your own machine. No rate limits, no API bill, and killing a process mid-run costs nothing. That makes it easy to test the unhappy path often, which is where most of the real bugs are.

The trade-off is that small local models are less predictable than hosted ones. Durable execution helps here because a bad step can be retried or inspected without redoing the whole run.

You can't trust what you can't see

Retries and resumes are invisible by default, and invisible failures are the hardest to debug. Sentry's tracing is a good fit, since a trace per step shows which call was slow, which one retried, and where a run picked back up.

A small React dashboard on top of the workflow history makes this easier still. Seeing a run's attempts as a timeline beats reading logs.

Open questions I'm still working through

  • How much state can sit in workflow history before replay gets slow?
  • Which failures should resume, and which should stop the run?
  • Does durability change how you write prompts and tool definitions?

I'll share more as I find answers.

articles.title: Are You a Python Developer or a Python Expert? 7 Tests I Failed Building 3 Desktop Apps

articles.body_html:
Description: Python security, screen capture, spring physics, HiDPI and PyInstaller .exe gotchas. 7 tests from shipping 3 no-telemetry Python apps for Windows (ATLOCK, ASNIPP, APIC).

Most Python developers can write a for loop, a Flask route and a pandas one-liner.

Python experts know what happens before line 1 runs, what Python can't do, and what breaks the moment your script leaves your laptop.

I found out which one I was while building three Windows desktop apps in pure Python: ATLOCK (a security suite), ASNIPP (a screenshot and screen recorder) and APIC (an image toolkit). No ads, no analytics SDKs, no bloat. Every test below is a real bug or design decision from one of them.

Score yourself honestly. 👇

Test 1: Do you know that import order can be a security decision? (ATLOCK)

Quick: what does import ctypes have to do with security?

On Windows, a DLL imported later can be loaded from the current directory. That is how DLL planting attacks work. The fix has to run before the other imports:

import sys, ctypes

if sys.platform == "win32":
    k32 = ctypes.WinDLL("kernel32", use_last_error=True)
    k32.SetDllDirectoryW.argtypes = [ctypes.c_wchar_p]
    k32.SetDllDirectoryW("")                      # drop the CWD from the DLL search path
    k32.SetDefaultDllDirectories.argtypes = [ctypes.c_uint32]
    k32.SetDefaultDllDirectories(0x1000)          # LOAD_LIBRARY_SEARCH_DEFAULT_DIRS

# only NOW import the heavy stuff
import cryptography, argon2

Developer: puts imports in alphabetical order.
Expert: knows import order is a runtime security boundary.

This is the very first thing that runs in ATLOCK, my pure-Python security suite.

Test 2: Can your screen recorder avoid recording itself? (ASNIPP)

I built a screen recorder with a floating control bar. First recording: the bar showed up in the video. 🤦

You don't need to hide and show windows. One Win32 call, straight from Python, does it:

import ctypes

def exclude_from_capture(widget):
    hwnd = int(widget.winId())
    # 0x11 = WDA_EXCLUDEFROMCAPTURE (Windows 10 2004+)
    ctypes.windll.user32.SetWindowDisplayAffinity(hwnd, 0x11)

The window stays visible to you and is invisible to every screen capture. That is how ASNIPP keeps its own toolbars, drawing overlay and recording border out of your videos.

Developer: crops the bar out in post.
Expert: knows ctypes gives Python the whole Windows API.

Test 3: Can your app decide what you meant, without asking? (APIC)

Good desktop software removes clicks. In APIC, my image toolkit, the rule is simple:

  • Drop one image → open it in the editor.
  • Drop many → open the batch converter. 
def on_files(self, paths: list[str]):
    if not paths:
        paths, _ = QFileDialog.getOpenFileNames(
            self, "Open Image(s)", "",
            "Images (*.png *.jpg *.jpeg *.webp *.bmp *.tiff *.gif *.ico *.heic *.avif)")
    if len(paths) == 1:
        self.open_in_edit(paths[0])
    elif paths:
        self.open_in_convert(paths)

def dropEvent(self, event):
    self.on_files([u.toLocalFile() for u in event.mimeData().urls()])

The home screen, the file dialog and drag-and-drop all go through one function. Add a new entry point and you add zero logic.

Developer: writes three code paths.
Expert: writes one funnel and lets every input flow into it. The UI is split into one module per mode (edit, convert, compress, search), and main.py only wires them together.

Test 4: Do you know the difference between "encrypted" and "encrypted correctly"? (ATLOCK)

Developer: AES.new(key, AES.MODE_ECB) and done.

Expert checklist:

  • AEAD, not just encryption: AES-256-GCM authenticates every chunk.
  • Slow KDF for passwords: Argon2id, not a bare SHA-256.
  • Never reuse a nonce with the same key.
  • Bind the header with AAD so metadata can't be swapped. 
import os
from argon2.low_level import hash_secret_raw, Type
from cryptography.hazmat.primitives.ciphers.aead import AESGCM

def seal(password: bytes, data: bytes) -> bytes:
    salt = os.urandom(16)
    key = hash_secret_raw(password, salt, time_cost=3, memory_cost=64 * 1024,
                          parallelism=4, hash_len=32, type=Type.ID)
    nonce = os.urandom(12)
    ct = AESGCM(key).encrypt(nonce, data, associated_data=b"v1")
    return salt + nonce + ct

(Simplified. ATLOCK's real container format also does chunking, key commitment and versioning.)

Test 5: Can you make a Qt animation feel alive with 6 lines of math? (ASNIPP)

ASNIPP's capture bar is a "Dynamic Island" that bounces open. Qt's built-in easing curves felt stiff, so I wrote a damped spring and plugged it into QEasingCurve:

import math
from PyQt6.QtCore import QEasingCurve

def spring(zeta, omega):
    wd = omega * math.sqrt(max(1e-6, 1 - zeta * zeta)) if zeta < 1 else 0.0
    def f(t):
        if t <= 0: return 0.0
        if t >= 1: return 1.0
        if zeta < 1:    # under-damped: overshoots, then settles (the bounce)
            return 1 - math.exp(-zeta * omega * t) * (math.cos(wd * t) + (zeta * omega / wd) * math.sin(wd * t))
        return 1 - math.exp(-omega * t) * (1 + omega * t)   # critically damped: no overshoot
    return f

BOUNCY = spring(0.66, 11.0)   # keep it at MODULE level (see below)

curve = QEasingCurve(QEasingCurve.Type.Linear)
curve.setCustomType(BOUNCY)

The trap: if the function is a temporary object, Python garbage-collects it while Qt still holds a pointer, and you get random crashes. Keep custom callables alive at module level. Only people who've been bitten know this one.

Test 6: Does your app look sharp on a 4K laptop with 150% scaling? (APIC)

Most Python GUI apps look blurry or oddly sized on modern displays. In Qt 6 the fix is one policy before you create the app:

from PyQt6.QtWidgets import QApplication
from PyQt6.QtCore import Qt

QApplication.setHighDpiScaleFactorRoundingPolicy(
    Qt.HighDpiScaleFactorRoundingPolicy.PassThrough)   # no rounding: 125%/150% stay crisp

app = QApplication(sys.argv)
app.setApplicationName("APIC")
app.setOrganizationName("Akhouri Systems")

PassThrough keeps fractional scales like 125% and 150% exact instead of snapping to 100% or 200%. Add one try/except AttributeError for older Qt builds, and your app looks native everywhere.

Developer: tests on their own monitor.
Expert: tests at 100%, 125%, 150% and 200%.

Test 7: Can you explain why Python can't truly erase a password from memory? (ATLOCK) 

password = "hunter2"
password = None   # is it gone? 🙂

No. Python str and bytes are immutable, and the interpreter is free to copy them. The best you can do is keep secrets in a mutable bytearray and wipe it explicitly:

buf = bytearray(b"hunter2")
# ... use it ...
for i in range(len(buf)):
    buf[i] = 0

An honest Python security tool says this out loud instead of promising magic. ATLOCK's source header lists what it can't do: memory wiping is best-effort, SSD shredding can't be guaranteed, and a same-user attacker can modify the script. Python experts document their limits.

Bonus: "Why does it work in VS Code and silently do nothing as a .exe?"

All three of my apps ship as Python compiled with PyInstaller (--onefile --windowed). It cost me an evening before I learned this: in a windowed build, sys.stdout and sys.stderr are None. Any print(), logging call or library traceback can fail silently, and your app "just doesn't open."

import sys, os

for name in ("stdout", "stderr"):
    if getattr(sys, name, None) is None:
        setattr(sys, name, open(os.devnull, "w", encoding="utf-8"))

# and show errors somewhere a human can see them:
import ctypes
ctypes.windll.user32.MessageBoxW(None, "Startup failed: ...", "App error", 0x10)

Try the code yourself

I'm the developer behind all of this, and the three apps are the proof that it works outside tutorials. They're built by Akhouri Systems, each is pure Python packaged as an .exe in a zip, with no ads and no analytics. The only network features are the ones you trigger yourself (for example ATLOCK's optional breach check, which sends only a 5-character hash prefix).

App Python lesson it proves What it is Get it
🔐 ATLOCK v5 Tests 1, 4, 7 Security suite: AES-256-GCM + Argon2id file guard, password vault, TOTP/FIDO2, anti-tamper Direct download (zip) · Microsoft Store
📸 ASNIPP v1 Tests 2, 5 Dynamic-Island-style screenshot, screen recorder, live drawing and editor Direct download (zip)
🖼️ APIC v1 Tests 3, 6 Image edit, convert, compress and search toolkit Direct download (zip)

If you're learning how Python behaves outside a notebook, run them and then ask what's going on under the hood. That's the fastest way I know to level up.

Your score

  • 0–2 tests known: You're a Python developer. Great start, now go break things.
  • 3–5: Solid. You've shipped something real.
  • 6–7: You're a Python expert. Come argue with me in the comments.

Which test did you fail first? Mine was the windowed-.exe one, and I lost an entire evening to it. Tell me yours below 👇
